newsitem.title: USA: USDA budget may pinch soil, export work - Glickman.
newsitem.headline: USDA budget may pinch soil, export work - Glickman.

text.p: Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman's forecast of a "lean...austere" budget may foreshadow cuts in popular farm export and soil conservation programs, analysts and congressional staff workers said Friday.

It also could mean accelerated closings and consolidation of the thousands of local Agriculture Department offices nationwide, they said. It would be highly difficult to cut the $5.8 billion earmarked for "Freedom to Farm" subsidies.
"I'm not sure they'd ever find their bones if they tried to do that," a House staff worker said, referring to the likely result of an attempt to curtail the farm support payments.

Budget negotiations were still under way but Glickman said on Thursday he anticipated "a lean but austere budget" that "protects our priorities" but imposed austerity on programs. He did not provide details.
Three analysts and two congressional staff workers said there were a half-dozen places where spending might be pared.

--Ag exports: Talk of eliminating "corporate welfare" could include another attempt to eliminate the $90 million a year Market Access Program despite reforms to limit the cost-sharing market development program to small businesses, trade groups and cooperatives.

Budget cutters also might aim at the Export Enhancement Program, the major U.S. export subsidy program. No subsidized U.S. grain sales have been made since mid-1995 but large amounts of EEP funds have been authorized in case of need;

--Conservation: Most frequently mentioned was reduction in the size of the 36.4 million-acre Conservation Reserve, which costs about $1.8 billion a year. Savings of $500 million-$700 million a year could be claimed through a smaller Conservaton Reserve and curtailing the new Environmental Quality Incentive Program, aimed at water purity.

Export promotion and the Conservation Reserve have many backers and have withstood many attacks in Congress. However, one analyst said both are harder to justify on budget terms because they no longer reduce farm subsidy costs. Under "Freedom to Farm," spending is fixed annually thorugh 2002.
"It's a new dynamic," the analyst said;

--Crop supports: One congressional staffer suggested lower loan rates as a way to save money. No one saw much support for a new on-farm grain storage plan or loan extensions because they would be costly. Glickman was mulling both ideas;

--Downsizing: A 1994 calls for merging a number of Agriculture Department agencies and closing hundreds of local offices. More closings could be imposed, analysts said, or the headquarters staff could be cut.
The White House budget office has suggested a merger of the Farm Service Agency, which runs the farm program, with the soil conservation agency. Glickman calls that step unlikely.

However, more consolidation could be argued as a way to reduce the chance of bias in farm loan programs, two analysts said. Black farmers complain of mistreatment at local offices, which are overseen by locally elected county committees.
--rural development. One staff worker suggested elimination of the $300 million Fund for Rural America. Created this year, it would aid ag research and rural economic development.
